body:
No Previous Policy

A. To be eligible for the LSW, individuals must meet all the following criteria

1 . No age requirement

2. Meet eligibility criteria for a Medicaid coverage group; and

o Individuals may qualify under a community Medicaid group for aged, blind or disabled persons, under a Special Income group, or under the Spenddown Waiver group ( 384-2 ).

3. Meets the level of care criteria as determined by the Division of Services for People with Disabilities (DSPD) ( 380-1 ).

Note - Individuals referred for the waiver who are not already on Medicaid or who have not already applied must file an application for Medicaid

B. Other Waiver Specific Rules for the LSW

1. Resources and Spousal Impoverishment (Assessment of Assets)

a. Married individuals applying for the Limited Supports Waiver, except those who will be on the MWI coverage group, need to have an assessment of assets completed, unless the individual's spouse does not meet the criteria of being a community spouse. Follow the rules in 573 for the assessment. Apply the spousal resource assessment to determine resource eligibility.

For individuals who were not in a nursing home or intermediate care facility prior to entering the LSW, set the assessment date as follows.

i. For individuals entering the waiver from a hospital, use the date of entry to the hospital as the assessment date. Ask the individual if he wants Medicaid coverage to pay for the hospital stay.

ii. Individuals entering the waiver from an assisted living facility, use the level of care date on the original 927 as the assessment date.

b. Single individuals must meet the aged, blind or disabled one-person asset test.

c. For any individual in the MWI group, see 384-1 MWI coverage group policy. Individuals eligible under the Limited Supports Waiver MWI category will not need an assessment of assets.

2. What does the member pay?

a. Members who qualify in the SSI, SSI Protected, 100% FPL, and Special Income groups will not have a contribution to the cost of care.

b. MWI members will have to pay an MWI premium.

c. Members who qualify in the Special Income group receive certain deductions from their total income to determine their cost-of-care. See section 431-16 for post-eligibility deductions.

d. Members with income over the special income limit (spenddown group) will receive the regular aged, blind or disabled deductions to determine their spenddown.

3. The PMV rule applies to LSW Members if someone else pays some or all of the Member's shelter and/or food costs. See section 415-10 .

· Does not apply to the Special Income Group

4. Transfer of Assets rules ( 575 ) apply only to the Special Income group, do not apply transfer of asset policies to any of the Community Medicaid Coverage groups or to the Spenddown Waiver group.

a. If a penalty period for a transfer of assets was in place while the individual was in a nursing home or intermediate care facility, the penalty period would not apply after the individual leaves the institution.

b. A penalty period that began while someone was in a medical institution continues to run. If the individual returns to an institution while the penalty period is still in effect, Medicaid will not cover the institutional costs.

c. If a Member eligible under the Special Income group transfers assets for less than fair market value resulting in a penalty period, that penalty period will carry over to eligibility under the Limited Supports Waiver until the end of the applicable penalty period. The Member would not be eligible for waiver services until the penalty period ends, but may qualify for regular Medicaid services.

body:
No Previous Policy

To be eligible for the Limited Supports Waiver (LSW), an individual must meet the criteria for one of the six eligibility coverage groups described below. There are two main categories: Community Medicaid groups and Institutional Medicaid groups.

A. Community Groups

Determine eligibility under regular community Medicaid groups before moving to Institutional groups.

o Members who meet the eligibility income and asset tests for a community group are eligible for LSW and will not have a post eligibility test to determine a contribution to the cost of care.

1. Income Eligibility for SSI recipients, SSI Protected Groups and Aged and Disabled 100% FPL group.

a. SSI recipients

An individual is income eligible if the individual meets the criteria found in section 329 .

b. SSI protected groups

An individual is income eligible if the individual meets the criteria under an SSI protected group. Follow the income policies for the specific protected group as referenced below except that you only count the individual's income. Do not deem income from a spouse.

An individual eligible for an SSI protected group will not have a contribution to the cost of care.

The SSI protected groups are:

o Disabled Adult Children ( 330-1 )

o 1619(a) and 1619(b) ( 330-2 )

o Eligible because of the Pickle Amendment ( 330-3 )

o Widows and Widowers ( 330-4 )

c. 100% of Poverty, Aged or Disabled (does not include spenddown group)

Individuals who do not receive SSI and are not in an SSI protected group may qualify under the poverty-level group if income is at or below 100% FPL.

i. A single individual meets income eligibility if the individual's countable income is at or below the 100% Poverty limit. See section 305 to determine countable income.

ii. For married individuals, count only the individual's income to determine eligibility. See section 305 to determine countable income except that you do not count the spouse's income. Countable income must be at or below the 100% Poverty limit for one person.

iii. A individual eligible for the 100% FPL group will not have a contribution to the cost of care.

iv. If the countable income of the individual exceeds 100% of the FPL and the individual has earned income, determine eligibility for the Medicaid Work Incentive. The individual may owe a premium to be eligible.

v. If the individual's countable income exceeds 100% of the FPL and the individual does not have earned income, decide if the individual is eligible under the Special Income group or the Spenddown Waiver group.

2. Income and Asset test for MWI (Medicaid Work Incentive - Individual must have earned income)

If the individual has earned income but does not receive SSI, does not meet SSI protected group eligibility, and does not pass the 100% FPL income tests, or does not pass the resource test for one of these groups, decide if the individual qualifies for the Medicaid Work Incentive.

a. Resources - Follow the resource rules in 314 to decide eligibility. Transfer of asset rules do not apply to this Medicaid group.

b. Income – Follow the income rules in 314 to decide eligibility and calculate the MWI premium. This is the amount the member must pay to be eligible for Medicaid.

c. If the member does not qualify for the Medicaid Work Incentive, determine eligibility under the Special Income Group or the Spenddown Waiver group.

B. Institutional Groups

1. Special Income Group

The special income group is for individuals who do not meet eligibility under community Medicaid groups, but would qualify if they were living in a medical institution because their income does not exceed the special income group limit.

a. Resource eligibility test

i. For single individuals, use the applicable resource limit found in section 503-2 for a one person ABD household size.

ii. For a married individual, apply the spousal impoverishment asset rules found in section 573 .

iii. Transfer of Assets rules apply to the Special Income coverage group.

b. Income eligibility test

An individual is eligible in the special income group if the individual's total income does not exceed 300% of the SSI payment rate. Determine income for the 300% of SSI test as follows:

i. Count only the individual's income. Do not deem income from the spouse.

ii. Do not count income that is excluded income according to section 463-1 .

iii. Compare total income to 300% of the SSI payment rate for one person.

iv. The individual is eligible if income does not exceed 300% of the SSI payment rate.

c. Post-Eligibility income process

After deciding a member's eligibility for the special income group, use the post eligibility test to decide how much a member must pay toward the cost-of-care.

i. Count only the individual's total income. Do not deem income from the spouse of a married member ( 463-1 ).

ii. Deduct from total income the post eligibility deductions listed in section 431-16 .

iii. The remaining amount is the member's contribution to cost-of-care.

2. Spenddown Waiver Group

The Spenddown Waiver group is for individuals who do not meet eligibility under regular community Medicaid groups or the Special Income Group.

a. Resources

i. For single individuals, use the applicable resource limit found in section 503-2 for a one person ABD household size.

ii. For a married individual, apply the spousal impoverishment asset rules found in section 573 .

iii. Transfer of asset rules do not apply to this Medicaid group.

b. Income

Count only the individual's income. The individual's total income must exceed 300% of the SSI payment level. A individual can qualify for the spenddown group if the individual's medical expenses would exceed the amount the individual would have to private pay. Deduct the following amounts to determine the individual's spenddown.

i. the ABD disregards in section 431-2 ,

ii. a deduction equal to 100% of the FPL and health insurance premiums described in 431-1 .

The remaining amount is the individual's spenddown. The individual may use medical bills as described in 461-5 to reduce or meet the spenddown.

body:
Contact DHHS Policy Specialist for Previous Policy

A. To be eligible, an individual must be screened for breast or cervical cancer by Utah Cancer Control Program (UCCP) and found to need treatment for breast or cervical cancer, or a precancerous condition. Individuals who have another type of cancer may be eligible if the primary cancer was breast or cervical cancer.

B. When an individual needs to be screened or has received a diagnosis from a medical provider other than a CDC contracted provider, refer them to UCCP to be screened for the Medicaid Cancer Program. The toll-free number is 1-800-717-1811.

C. UCCP will complete and sign a Medicaid Cancer Program Referral, Form 928, to verify that an individual has been screened and found to need treatment for breast or cervical cancer, or a pre-cancerous condition.

D. An individual who has moved to Utah can be eligible for the Medicaid Cancer Program if they were diagnosed by a CDC provider. Have the CDC provider verify:

· If the person still needs treatment.

· If they have breast or cervical cancer or a pre-cancerous condition.

· The diagnosis date.

Use this link to find CDC screeners: https://cancer.utah.gov/

body:
Previous Policy

An individual is not eligible for the Medicaid Cancer Program if the individual is enrolled in or is eligible for certain health coverage. Applicants who provide necessary verifications, cooperate with medical support enforcement (if applicable-see 227 ), and are found eligible for other Medicaid programs are not eligible for the Medicaid Cancer Program. If the applicant does not submit all the necessary verifications to determine eligibility for other Medicaid programs, and they qualify for the Medicaid Cancer Program, approve the Medicaid Cancer Program.

Medicaid

Adults are not eligible for the Medicaid Cancer Program if the qualify for other programs. Some of the other Medicaid programs include:

Parent and Caretaker Relative;

Pregnant Woman; and

Adult Expansion.

If individuals are Medicaid Cancer Program eligible, do not put them on:

Targeted Adult Medicaid;

Medically Needy programs; or

Refugee Medical Assistance.

Armed Forces

An individual who is eligible for health coverage provided by the Armed Forces is not eligible for the Medicaid Cancer program.

Medicare

An individual who is enrolled in Part A or Part B Medicare is not eligible for the Medicaid Cancer program.

Health Insurance or Group Health Plan

An individual enrolled in any health insurance or a group health plan is not eligible for the Medicaid Cancer Program unless:

· The plan does not provide benefits for cancer treatment.

· The plan is limited coverage even if the plan covers the cancer treatment. Limited coverage plans are insurance plans that only provide medical care for a single type of service or specific disease, under special circumstances, or where the medical care is secondary to the primary purpose of the insurance (i.e., medical under automobile insurance.)

· The coverage is under the Indian Health Services.

There is no sanction or waiting period if an applicant terminates their health insurance coverage.

E. Co-Pays

Individuals on the Medicaid Cancer Program are not required to pay co-pays.

body:
Contact DHHS Policy Specialist for Previous Policy

Retroactive Coverage

Eligibility for retroactive coverage can begin the third month before the application month, but no earlier than the month in which the individual is screened for breast and/or cervical cancer. CDC must either do the screening and diagnosis or review the screening and diagnosis, and confirm the need for treatment of breast and/or cervical cancer. (See 390-1 )

Eligibility Period

1. For an individual diagnosed with a pre-cancerous condition, the eligibility period can be approved for up to 3 months starting with the month the screening is completed.

2. For an individual diagnosed with breast or cervical cancer the eligibility period can be up to 12 months.

3. An individual is not limited to one period of eligibility. Eligibility can be renewed at the annual or 3 month review. (See 390-4 for review requirements.)

4. If an individual’s Cancer program closes, they may reapply and receive a new period of eligibility and coverage if they have been screened and determined by the CDC program to need treatment of breast or cervical cancer, or a pre-cancerous condition and meets all other eligibility criteria.

body:
Medical Condition

The TB Positive program is for individuals who are infected with tuberculosis or are suspected of being infected with tuberculosis.

Eligibility for Other Medicaid Coverage Groups

An individual who is eligible for any Medicaid program without a spenddown or MWI premium is not eligible for the TB Positive Group.

Other Medicaid Requirements

The general eligibility requirements apply. Individuals must:

Complete an application

Be a state resident

Be a US citizen or eligible non-citizen

Income

Determine household size and income using MAGI methodology (Sections 401-1 , 401-2 and 401-3 ). The income limit is equal to the earned income break-even point for SSI eligibility. ( Table II ) Deduct 5% of the FPL for the applicable household size to determine if the individual is under the income limit.

Resources

There is no asset test for this coverage group.

Restriction on Medical Services

Those individuals infected with TB who are eligible under other Medicaid programs receive the full Medicaid Scope of Services. Members eligible for the TB Positive Group program receive a more limited range of benefits for treatment of their tuberculosis.

Section 1902(z) (2) of the Act describes the scope of services for this program:

Prescribed drugs

Physicians’ services and services described in section 1905(a)(2)

Laboratory and X-ray services (including services to confirm the presence of infection)

Clinic services and federally-qualified health center services

Case management services (as defined in section 1915(g)(2))

Services (other than room and board) designed to encourage completion of regimens of prescribed drugs by outpatients, including services to observe directly the intake of prescribed drugs.

To be covered, these services must be related to the treatment of tuberculosis.

body:
Previous Policy

The Refugee Resettlement Program (RRP) provides Federal funding for medical assistance. Refugee Medical Assistance (RMA), is available to refugees for up to 8 months beginning with the month of the date of entry. See section 394-3 to determine the date of entry.

Adults are not eligible for RMA if they qualify for other programs without a premium or a spenddown, such as: Parent and Caretaker Relative, Pregnant Woman, Targeted Adult Medicaid, Medicaid Cancer Program, Adult Expansion Program.

If an individual is eligible for RMA, do not put them on Medically Needy programs.

RMA is available for refugees who: Meet immigration status ( 394-2 ). Provide the name of the resettlement agency. Are not full-time students in institutions of higher education unless approved by the state as part of an employment plan.

RMA is also available to Iraqi and Afghan Special Immigrants. Treat Iraqi and Afghan Special Immigrants like refugees; they are not subject to the 5–year bar. RMA eligibility for Iraqi and Afghan Special Immigrants begins with the month of their date of entry or adjusted status (See 205-2 ) .

RMA is available for children born in the US to mothers on RMA coverage, follow these rules when approving RMA for these children. When a woman on RMA coverage becomes pregnant, check to see if she is eligible for Medicaid. A child born to a mother on Utah Medicaid is automatically eligible for a full year of coverage. RMA is NOT a Medicaid program, so a child born to a mother who is only eligible for RMA is not eligible for that full year of coverage. Once the child is born to a mother on RMA, consider Medicaid coverage for the child. If the child is not eligible for a Medicaid program, CHIP, or UPP the child may be given RMA coverage along with the mother (See section 394-2 ).

heading: Effective Date: August 1, 2026

body:
Previous Policy

1. Determine eligibility for RMA if:

· The adult refugee does not qualify for Medicaid without cost or

· The child does not qualify for Medicaid without cost, CHIP, or UPP, and

· The date of application is within 8 months of the date of entry.

(For Iraqi and Afghan Special Immigrants, use either the date of entry, or the date they were granted Special Immigrant status, whichever one is later.)

2. Re-determine RMA eligibility using the income and assets held on the date of the original medical assistance application if a refugee listed in 394-2 loses Medicaid eligibility within the available RMA eligibility timeframe for one of the following reasons:

· Increased earnings or assets

· Categorical ineligibility (e.g. a member receiving Adult Expansion who loses coverage for failing to comply with ESI requirements).

3. For all members including Iraqi and Afghan Special Immigrants, close RMA at the end of the 8 th month. Once the program is closed, determine eligibility for Medicaid, CHIP or UPP. Treat Iraqi and Afghan Special Immigrants as qualified non-citizens; the 5-year bar does not apply.

body:
Contact DHHS Policy Specialist for Previous Policy

For a full list of status codes see:

Alien Quick Reference Status Chart

To be eligible for RMA, a person must have one of these statuses (all are considered refugees under RMA):

A person who is a refugee under Section 207 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).

A person who has been granted political asylum under Section 208 of the INA.

A person who has been paroled under Section 212(d)(5) of the INA as a refugee or asylee.

A Cuban or Haitian entrant.

Amerasian Immigrants.

Children of a refugee family who are born in the U.S. These children have the same non-citizen registration number as their mother with a suffix of 01, 02 etc. The suffix shows the sequence of birth in the U.S. These children are eligible for RMA if not eligible for any other Medicaid program. See 394 .

Non-citizens certified as Victims of Severe Forms of Trafficking. These non-citizens have been certified by the Federal Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) and have been issued a Certification Letter.

Certain family members of Victims of a Severe Form of Trafficking.

Iraqi or Afghan Special Immigrant Status granted under section 101(a)(27) of the INA.

body:
Previous Policy

Base eligibility for RMA on the applicant’s income and assets on the date of application. Do not consider any increases in income or assets after the date of application.

A. Income

Follow the income rules for Medically Needy Family to determine the countable income ( 441 ).

If, on the application, the countable income is equal to or less than the BMS for the household size, the household is eligible for RMA without a spenddown through the end of the 8 month period.

If the countable income is more than the BMS for the household size the household may spenddown ( 461 ).

Do not increase the spenddown if household income increases.

Decrease the spenddown if household income decreases.

If the income decreases below the BMS the household does not spenddown through the end of the 8 month period.

Assets

Follow the asset rules for Medically Needy Family to determine the countable assets and the asset limit. Use the assets held on the date of application to decide eligibility. Any asset increase has no effect on eligibility.

Contact a DHHS Policy Specialist for Previous Policy

Use the Refugee Sponsor Contribution Form 1043 to contact the sponsor and verify sponsor contributions to the refugee. Send a copy of the completed form to the resettlement agency.

Refugee Sponsor

Count any cash contributions from a sponsor.

Do not count the sponsor's income or assets.

Do not count in-kind services or shelter provided by the sponsor to the refugee.

Resettlement Agencies

Do not count any cash or in-kind benefits received from the resettlement agencies or under a matching grant program as noted on the form 1043.

One-time reception placement in-kind benefits from local resettlement agencies under the Department of State or Department of Justice Reception and Placement programs are excluded for all medical assistance programs.

One-time reception placement payments received in cash are excluded as income for Refugee Medicaid. Cash payments for one-time reception placement are countable for Medicaid and CHIP programs.

A. General Rules

The first step to determine eligibility for MAGI-based coverage groups is to build the MAGI household for each applicant or recipient. The household composition rules follow federal tax rules, and in some cases, relationship rules.

body:
B. Applicant and Recipient Requirements

1. An applicant or recipient must declare whether they intend to file a federal tax return for the year in which Medicaid eligibility is being determined, and whether the person can be claimed as a dependent by another tax filer.

2. If the individual expects to file a tax return and cannot be claimed as a dependent, the individual must state:

a. who they expect to claim as dependents and the relationships of those individuals whom they are claiming

b. who lives in the home and their relationship to those individuals, and

c. any anticipated changes in the coming tax year.

3. If a tax filer expects to claim a relative who is not a dependent child or who is an unrelated individual, the tax filer may need to verify the reason that person can be claimed as a dependent if the information the agency receives conflicts with the client's statement.

4. If an applicant does not intend to file a tax return, the individual must declare who lives in the home and the relationship of those individuals.

5. Household size is determined separately for each individual applying for benefits.

The following sections define how to determine household size for tax filers, dependents and non-tax filers.

body:
Effective Date: November 1, 2021

Previous Policy (234-1 was renumbered to 401-2 as of November 1, 2021)

A. Definitions

The following definitions apply for MAGI households.

1. "Child" means a biological, adopted or step-child.

2. “ Dependents ” are people for whom a tax filer generally provides support; they may be children or other relatives. The tax filer may be able to claim tax credits for certain dependents.

3. "MAGI household" means the household size and composition for someone whose Medicaid eligibility is determined using the MAGI methodology.

4. "Parent" means a biological, adoptive or step-parent.

5. "Sibling" means a biological, adoptive, half-sibling, or step-sibling who meets the age limits, and school attendance requirement, if applicable.

6. "Tax Household" means the number of individuals included on a tax filer's tax return whom the tax filer can claim as dependents.

B. Tax household rules

The MAGI household uses tax rules about who is part of a tax filer's household with some exceptions.

The following information defines who can be counted in a tax filer's tax household . This is to help establish an understanding of the tax rules about households, which will be the basis for how to build the MAGI household for Medicaid.

1. The tax filer . This is the individual who is applying for Medicaid, states an intent to file a tax return, and is not being claimed as a dependent by another tax filer.

2. The spouse of a tax filer is included in the tax household if the couple files a joint return. In essence, they are both filers. ( NOTE : Spouses living together are always included in each other's MAGI household for Medicaid even if the couple does not file a joint return, which is discussed in section C. Unmarried couples are not allowed to file a joint tax return. (See common-law marriage policy in C.2.)

3. Dependents include the following:

a. Child. To be a qualifying child for the purpose of claiming a tax credit, the child must:

· Be under age 19, or age 19 through 23 and enrolled in school full-time, or be a child of any age who is totally and permanently disabled. If the individual says he can claim the disabled child, accept the client's statement.

· Not have provided 50% of his own support. The child may be claimed by the parent he lives with, or in some cases by the non-custodial parent.

· Be the tax filer's son, daughter, stepchild, foster child, brother, sister, half-brother, half-sister, stepbrother, stepsister, or a descendent of any of them. An adopted child is treated as the tax filer's child, including a child placed for adoption with the tax filer, as tax law makes no distinction between children who are adopted and those who are still in the adoption process.

· Be younger than either the tax filer or the tax filer's spouse.

· Live with the tax filer more than half of the year (some exceptions apply for temporary absence, children who were born or who died during the year, and when parents are divorced.)

b. Others who live with the tax filer the whole year and is someone who must meet the following criteria:

· Is a relative of the filer or the filer's spouse, or is an unrelated person; and

· Cannot be the tax filer's child or a child of another taxpayer, (so a child who does not meet the criteria to be a qualifying child may be claimed as a dependent relative); and

· Is not expected to have income in excess of the income limit for dependents see table VII ; and

· The tax filer expects to provide more than 50% of the person's support.

c. Other relatives who do not live with the tax filer and is someone who must meet the following criteria:

· Is one of the listed relatives of the filer or the filer's spouse;

· Cannot be the tax filer's child or a child of another taxpayer, (so a child who does not meet the criteria to be a qualifying child may be claimed as a dependent relative); and

· Is not expected to have income in excess of the income limit for dependents see table VII ; and

· The tax filer expects to provide more than 50% of the person's support.

Note: Death or divorce does not change relationships that were established by marriage.

C. MAGI Medicaid household ("MAGI Household") for tax filers

The MAGI household for a tax filer is determined by following tax rules about household composition with some modifications specifically for Medicaid.

A tax filer's household can include individuals who are not typically included in a Medicaid household, such as children age 19-23. That is because the MAGI household follows tax rules about who is included in the MAGI household size. Therefore, it is possible for the MAGI household to include a foster child, an adult child, or a dependent person who is not the spouse or child of the tax filer. In addition, dependents claimed by a tax filer may not always live with the tax filer.

1. MAGI Household size for a tax filer.

a. To determine the MAGI household size for an applicant or recipient who expects to file a federal tax return and cannot be claimed as a dependent by another tax filer, use his tax household (Section B.) with the following additions. (If the filer is a child who lives with parents who will not file a tax return, see 401-3 .)

i. Include a spouse living with the tax filer who is not part of the tax household because the spouse is filing a separate return or is not filing a return.

· If the couple files a joint return, the spouse is already counted in the tax household and therefore is counted in the MAGI household.

· Married couples that are permanently separated, not living together, and filing a joint tax return, will be treated as non-tax filers. The MAGI household will not include the absent spouse.

ii. Include the expected number of unborn children of anyone counted in the tax filer's MAGI household who is pregnant at the time of application or renewal.

Example 1 : John, age 23, attends the university full time. He lives with his mother, Jessica, and his 17-year-old sister, Chris. John works 15 hours per week, earning minimum wage. His mother provides more than 50% of his support. She claims John and Chris as qualifying children on her taxes. Chris is pregnant. Jessica's MAGI household includes herself, John, Chris and Chris' unborn child. Jessica is able to claim them as dependents for the purposes of determining her Medicaid household.

Example 2 : Mary is applying for Medicaid. She has three children: Vanessa, a 19-year-old full-time college student, Trudy age 15 and Miriam age 17. Vanessa works 20 hours per week, earning minimum wage. Her mother states she provides 50% of Vanessa's support. Mary can claim Vanessa as her dependent. Mary's MAGI household includes herself, Vanessa, Trudy and Miriam. Due to the amount that she earns, Vanessa will be expected to be required to file a tax return. Her income will count as part of the household income.

b. Accept the client's statement about filing a tax return.

c. Accept the client's statement about a pregnancy and the expected number of unborn children.

d. Accept the client's statement about dependents he expects to claim unless the agency has information that conflicts with the client's statement.

i. If the agency has information that is not reasonably compatible with the client's statement about claiming someone as a dependent, ask the tax filer for information supporting their statement.

ii. If the tax filer cannot establish a reasonable explanation of why someone can be claimed as a dependent, do not count that person in the tax filer's MAGI household. For example, if the tax filer claims an unrelated person as a dependent, but that person's income exceeds (or is expected to exceed) the limit for a dependent, do not count that person in the tax filer's MAGI household.

2. MAGI Household size for the spouse of a tax filer.

a. Joint filers who live together.

If a married couple files a joint tax return, the MAGI household for the tax filer's spouse is the same as the MAGI household for the tax filer. (They are actually both considered filers.)

b. Separate filers who live together .

i. The MAGI household for a spouse who files a separate tax return includes:

· Both spouses who are living together but are filing separate returns;

· The number of dependents the individual expects to claim as exemptions on his own return; and

· The expected number of unborn children of anyone included in his MAGI household.

ii. If a spouse is living with his parent who is claiming him as a dependent child, follow rules for children of a tax filer.

iii. If a spouse will not be claimed on a joint return with his spouse, will not be claimed as a dependent by another tax filer, and will not file a return himself, follow the rules for non-filers to determine his MAGI household ( 401-3 ).

iv. Utah does not recognize common-law marriages unless they have received a certificate from a court, in which case, they are married.

v. An unmarried couple who states they are filing taxes jointly (as in the case of a self-stated common law marriage), will be treated as non-tax filers.

· Utah will allow a couple to file a joint tax return if they entered into a common-law marriage in a state that recognizes such relationships and who later moved to Utah.

· Take the client's statement unless the agency has conflicting information.

3. MAGI household of children of a tax filer

Build the household separately for each child living with the applicant tax filer based on the situation for each child. Children in the same household may have different MAGI household sizes.

When divorced or separated parents have joint custody, see 401-4 to determine the child's residence. The child's MAGI household will be determined based on where the child lives and the following rules.

a. If the child meets the criteria of being a child and lives with only two parents who file a joint return and claim an exemption for the child, the child's MAGI household size is the same as the parents' MAGI household size with one addition:

· If the child is married and also lives with his spouse, include the child's spouse in the child's MAGI household size.

b. If the child meets the criteria of being a child and lives with only one parent who claims the child on her tax return, the child's MAGI household is the same as the parent's MAGI household size with one addition:

· If the child is married and also lives with his spouse, include the child's spouse in the child's MAGI household size.

c. If the child meets the criteria of a being a qualifying child and lives with two parents, but the parents will not file a joint tax return, then the MAGI household size of that child does not follow the tax filer's household size. The household size follows non-tax-filer rules ( 401-3 ).

d. A child could live with two biological (or adoptive) parents and a step-parent (someone married to one of the biological parents). In this case, the biological parents will not be filing a joint return, so determine the child's MAGI household following non-tax filer rules.

e. If the child meets the criteria of a being a child and lives with one parent, but a non-custodial parent will claim the child on his or her tax return, the MAGI household size of the child does not follow the tax filer's household size. Use non-tax-filer rules (401-3).

4. Child applying on her own

A child who meets the age criteria to be a child of a tax filer may apply for Medicaid on her own if she does not live with her parents. If she expects to be permanently absent from her parents' home, the agency will not consider her as her parents' tax dependent to determine her eligibility.

· Decide if she expects to file her own return and use the applicable rules to build her MAGI household. (Tax filer rules if she expects to file; non-tax filer rules if she does not expect to file ( 401-3 ).

· Count only her income and that of anyone who is included in her household, if applicable.

5. MAGI household for other dependents of a tax filer

Use the non-tax filer rules to determine the household size for the following tax dependents ( 401-3 ):

· An “other relative” claimed as a dependent of a tax filer who is not the spouse or dependent child of the filer (defined in B.3.b and c)­;

· A “child” who is not the tax filer's child (defined in B.3.a);

· A child placed for adoption before the adoption is finalized.

o Tax law allows a tax filer to claim the prospective adopted child as a child. However, Utah Code does not recognize the adopting parent as a legal parent until the process is complete.

B. Temporary Absence

1. When a child is in Division of Child and Family Services (DCFS) or Juvenile Justice and Youth Services (JJYS) custody, the child is not considered temporarily absent.

2. MAGI-Based and Family Medically Needy programs : An individual is temporarily absent if:

a. The individual lives away from home because of work, education, medical care, military service, vacation, incarceration or some other temporary purpose (example: volunteer services for a church or the Peace Corps) and

b. The individual intends to return to the home when the reason for the absence ends.

3. There is no time limit for a temporary absence as long as the family member intends to return to the home.

a. If the absent family member changes their intent so that they do not intend to return, they are no longer temporarily absent. They are no longer a member of the household at the point that their intent changes or if there are factors conflicting with Utah Residency, see 207-5 .

b. If there are factors conflicting with Utah Residency see 207-1 .

c. If the absent family member is in a medical institution, see 215-4 and 463 to determine that person's eligibility and cost of care.

4. MAGI related programs :

a. Tax filer household : A person may be absent from the household and still count as a household member .

· See section 401-2 for permanently separated spouses who file a joint return.

b. Non-filer households: a person would have to live in the household or be temporarily absent to be included in the household size.

c. Regardless of tax filing status, when a member is an incarcerated individual of a public institution such as a jail or prison, take the client’s statement that the individual is temporarily absent.

Exception: If the incarcerated individual is a child and the parent’s rights have been terminated, they are not considered temporarily absent.

If the other parent has an open medical assistance case, refer to 815-4 about adding a new household member to re-determine the child's eligibility.

Previous Policy (401-5 was previously found in 476-5 until November 1, 2021)

A. General Requirements

There are no special considerations to determine Medicaid eligibility for households that contain both eligible and ineligible non-citizen members.

B. Non-Emergency Medicaid Programs

1. Follow the rules for the program type for which you are determining eligibility.

· For MAGI-based coverage groups , follow the rules on how to build the MAGI household ( 401 through 401-3 ).

· For Medically Needy Family programs , follow the rules found in sections 404-1 through 404-4 .

· For ABD programs , follow the rules found in 408-1 through 408-6 .

2. Do not include ineligible non-citizen family members in the coverage for non-emergency Medicaid, but count them in the household size.

C. Emergency Medicaid Programs

1. Follow the income deeming and household size rules for the program for which you are determining eligibility.

· For MAGI-based coverage groups , follow the rules on how to build the MAGI household ( 401 through 401-3 ).

· For Medically Needy Family programs , follow the rules found in sections 404-1 through 404-4 .

· For ABD programs , follow the rules found in 408-1 through 408-6 .

2. Do not deem income from a non-citizen's sponsor who is not a spouse or parent living with the non-citizen on an Emergency Medicaid case ( 205-4 , 205-5 ).

3. Do not include any U.S. citizen or qualified non-citizen family member in the coverage for an Emergency Medicaid program. Family members who are U.S. citizens or qualified non-citizens may count in the household size for the ineligible non-citizen seeking emergency Medicaid.

body:
Previous Policy (402-1 was previously found in 345 until November 1, 2021)

A. PCR Household Composition

The PCR program follows the MAGI methodology to determine the adult’s household composition ( 401-1 ). Sections 345 , 345-1 and 345-2 explain the other program requirements. The household size is used to determine if the countable income falls within the program income limit for the individual ( Table VII ).

1. Adults qualify for the PCR program if they meet the program requirements stated in 345 , and the income requirements found in 440-1 through 440-5 .

2. Include the following individuals in the PCR household:

a. Adults: Both of the married parents living in the home will be included in the household.

i. An unmarried couple generally cannot be part of each other’s MAGI household. They must each have their own case.

· If the parents are unmarried and live together, they can both receive PCR if they meet the criteria in 345.

ii. If one parent of the unmarried couple is a tax filer and claiming the other parent as a "tax dependent" on their tax return ( 401 ), the tax dependent would be part of the tax-filer's household. However, the tax-filer would not be included in the other parent's Medicaid household.

b. Children: Dependent children who are included in the MAGI household.

i. Children are dependent if they meet the age criteria ( 345-1 ).

ii. A child living with a tax filing parent, who is not claimed as a tax dependent, cannot be included in the parent’s PCR household ( 401-2 ).

iii. If unmarried parents have only one child in common, that child can qualify each of the parents for coverage.

iv. Unborn children are always included in a married couple’s PCR household.

v. An Unborn child can be included in a self-declared father’s household in the following situation:

1. The woman is in the third trimester of the pregnancy, and

2. The presumed father acknowledges paternity of the unborn by completing the Form 941.

c. Non-parent caretaker relatives : Both the caretaker relative and spouse can be eligible for the PCR program if they meet the criteria in all sections included in 345 . Their MAGI household will include both spouses and their tax dependents.

i. The caretaker relatives may or may not be claiming the dependent, deprived relative children in their care as tax dependents.

ii. If the caretaker relative is not a tax filer, their household will follow the rules in 401-4 .

iii. If the caretaker relative is not a tax filer and does not claim the children as tax dependents, the caretaker relative’s MAGI household will follow the rules in 401-3 .

B. PCR Multi-Generational Households

In certain circumstances, a non-parent caretaker relative could assume primary responsibility for the dependent child's care while the child’s parent is in the home.

1. Follow the MAGI methodology and the program requirements as stated in A.1.

2. Allow the household to decide who has the primary responsibility for the child's care on a case by case basis.

a. If the parent is living in the home, the presumption is that the parent is providing most of the care to the child. However, if the non-parent caretaker relative claims to be the primary caregiver, accept that statement.

b. If the parent and the caretaker relative provide conflicting statements about who is the primary caretaker, consider the parent the primary caretaker.

c. The same dependent child cannot qualify both a parent and a non-parent caretaker relative for PCR Medicaid.

d. The child must still be deprived of support ( 345-2 ).

Example #1: Tammy Baker is a 19-year-old mother. She and her 18-month-old son, Blake, live with Tammy's mother, Sue. Tammy goes to school full-time while her mother cares for Blake. Sue is divorced and claims both Tammy and Blake as tax dependents. Sue says she is the primary caretaker for Blake. Since Blake is deprived of support and Sue does most of the care giving, Sue can be considered as the caretaker relative for Blake.

Child Medicaid Household Composition

The Child program follows the MAGI methodology to determine the child’s household composition ( 401-1 ). Section 347 explains the age criteria and other program requirements. The household size is used to determine if the countable income falls within the program income limit for the individual ( Table VII ).

1. Children who live in a two-parent joint filing household will have the same household composition as their parents.

2. Children who meet one of the exceptions found in 401-3 will follow the non-tax filer (relationship) rules, and the following people will be included in the child’s household:

· Parents,

· Siblings,

· Child’s spouse and,

· Child’s children.

A. MAGI-Based Foster Care Household Composition

Non-IV-E Foster Care programs follow the MAGI Non-tax filer rules to determine the child’s household composition ( 401-3 ). Sections 354 through 354-5 explain the different requirements. The household size is used to determine if the countable income falls within the program income limit for the individual ( Table VII ).

1. For non-tax-filers, the foster child is not included in the household.

2. The foster care child will be opened on a separate medical assistance case.

B. All Other Medical Assistance Coverage Groups

· Do not include a child who has been placed in the home under a Foster Care program in the household size. A child who is in Foster Care must have their own Medicaid case.

Note: This applies to a Foster Care child who has been placed with a Foster Care family. This does not refer to a Foster Care child who has been placed with their own parent or other Specified Relative under a "Preliminary Placement" by DCFS ( 354 ).

body:
Previous Policy (404-1 was previously found in 345 D until November 1, 2021)

A. Household Structure for the Family Medically Needy Program

The Parents and Caretaker Relatives Family Needy program is also known as the Family Medically Needy. Family relationships are used to determine who must be included in the same Medicaid household. A person may be counted in the household size even though the person does not qualify for coverage under the medically needy program. A child may be counted in the household size but receive benefits under the MAGI Child Medicaid program if the household income is within the limits of that program.

1. Spouses, parents and dependent children who live together are counted in the household size.

a. Do not include a parent, step-parent or adoptive parent who receives SSI in the household size.

b. For a parent to be eligible, there must be a dependent child in the household ( 345-1 ). The child must be deprived of parental support ( 345-2 ).

2. Do not count a child who receives SSI in the household size. The child may meet the criteria of being a dependent child to qualify a parent for coverage even if there are no other dependent children in the home.

3. Count an adopted child who receives a Federal, State or Local government special needs adoption payment in the household size. The child must meet the criteria in 345-1 and 345-2 . A subsidized adoption child cannot receive coverage under Family Medically Needy ( 355 ).

4. Count an unborn child, or children, of a pregnant woman in the household size. The unborn child may be considered a dependent child in the third trimester to qualify her for the Family Medically Needy program, if there are no other dependent children in the home.

5. The unmarried father of an unborn child may receive Family Medically Needy if he:

a. is living in the home with the pregnant woman who is in her third trimester; and

b. has acknowledged paternity on Form 941.

Do not include the unmarried father in the same Medicaid household as the pregnant woman.

A. Pregnant Woman Medically Needy Household Composition

1. Family relationships are used to determine who must be included in the same Medicaid household. A person may be counted in the household size even though the person is not included in the Pregnant Woman Medically Needy program. Section 349 provides the Pregnant Woman Medically Needy program requirements. The household size is used to determine what countable income is used to determine the amount of the spenddown ( Table VII ).

2. Spouses and dependent children who live together are counted in the household size.

a. Do not include a parent, step-parent or adoptive parent who receives SSI in the household size.

b. Do not count a child who receives SSI in the household size.

3. Count an unborn child, or children, of a pregnant woman in the household size. The unborn child may be considered a dependent child in the third trimester to qualify her for the Family Medically Needy program, if there are no other dependent children in the home.

4 . Do not include the unmarried father in the same Medicaid household as the pregnant woman.

Foster Care Non-IV-E Medically Needy Household Composition

1. Children who do not meet IV-E foster care criteria when being taken into state custody, but have income in excess of the income limit for the MAGI Based Non-IV-E foster care programs, may qualify for a medically needy program. Section 354 provides the Foster Care Medically Needy program requirements.

2. Do not include a foster child, placed in a foster home, in the foster family’s household size.

3. A child who is in foster care must have their own Medicaid case.

4. If siblings are placed together in a foster home, they can be in the same Medicaid household. See section 404-6 for sibling deeming rules.

Note: This does not refer to a foster care child who has been placed with their own parent or other non-parent caretaker relative under a "Preliminary Placement" by DCFS ( 354 ).

body:
Previous Policy (404-5 was previously found in 476-1 until November 1, 2021)

A. Financial Responsibility

Refer to the applicable policy in section 404 to determine household size for medically needy coverage.

1. Financial responsibility for medically needy coverage is limited to a spouse for a spouse and parents for their dependent children. Policy prohibits the deeming of a child's income and assets to a parent.

2. Policy prohibits the deeming of a sibling's income and assets to another sibling.

3. Do not count income of an unmarried partner to determine eligibility of a parent, even if they have one or more dependent children in common.

B. Whose Income to Count

Count income as follows for family members who are living together:

1. To determine eligibility for either the parent or the parent's spouse on Family Medically Needy, count income of both the parent and the parent's spouse.

2. To determine eligibility for a child on either Family or Child Medically Needy, count the income of both the child and the child's parents, but not the child's siblings. (See 415-5 for child support payments; 415-1 for unearned income; 419-5 for income that is excluded for a child.)

a. If a child meeting the age criteria is emancipated, continue to count the parents' income.

b. Count income of a child's spouse, if applicable.

c. Do not count income of a non-parent caretaker.

3. A parent, stepparent or adoptive parent who receives SSI cannot be included in the household size and their income and assets will not be counted in determining eligibility for family-related Medicaid.

4. To determine eligibility for a woman on Pregnant Woman Medically Needy, count income of the pregnant woman and her spouse.

a. If a pregnant woman is under age 18 and living with her parents, count her parent's income ( 405-1 ).

b. If a pregnant woman is between the age of 18 and 19, living with her parents, does not meet dependent child criteria 402-3 , and fails the MAGI-based Pregnant Woman program, count only her income and that of her spouse. 405-3 )

5. Count the income of the unmarried father of an unborn child only to determine his eligibility for Family Medically Needy Medicaid.

· If he is under age 18 and living with his parents, or 18 and meets dependent child criteria, count his parents' income, too.

6. Temporary absence or status as an ineligible non-citizen does not change how to count income from that person ( 401-4 , 401-5 ).

Follow the policy found in 401-4 to determine how to apply policy for temporary absence situations.

A. MAGI-Based Groups and Minor Parents

1. Determine eligibility for Child Medicaid for the minor parent under age 19 living with their parents ( 347 ).

2. If a woman is under age 19, pregnant, living with a parent and is not eligible for Child Medicaid, consider eligibility for Pregnant Woman Medicaid ( 349 ).

B. Medically Needy Family, Child or Pregnant Woman

A parent under age 19 who does not qualify for a MAGI-based coverage group, may qualify under a medically needy coverage group.

1. A minor parent is defined as a parent who is under age 18, or who is between the ages of 18 and 19.

2. Eligibility is determined based upon the minor parent's age, student status, deprivation and living arrangements (See 345-1 , 345-2 and 401-4 ).

body:
Previous Policy (405-2 was previously found in 465-1 until November 1, 2021)

For the Medically Needy Family, Child and Pregnant Woman programs, the eligibility of a minor parent under the age 18 depends on where the individual is living.

1. When a pregnant woman under age 18 lives with her parents or stepparents, the parents’ income and assets must be deemed to her when determining her eligibility for Medically Needy Medicaid. It does not matter if the woman is emancipated. As long as she lives with her parents, the parents’ income and assets must be deemed to her when determining her eligibility.

a. Include the unborn child in the household size.

b. Only count the income and assets of the father of the unborn child, if the father is married to the mother of the unborn and living in the home.

Example : 16-year-old Mary is pregnant and lives with her parents. Her boyfriend is also living with this family and Mary states he is the father of the unborn child. Her boyfriend has not signed the Form 941 and they have no other child in common. The boyfriend's income or assets are not countable when determining Mary's eligibility for Family Medically Needy Medicaid.

2. When determining eligibility for the pregnant minor's boyfriend who is the father of the unborn and living in the home, the following apply:

a. Only count his income and assets to determine his Medicaid eligibility.

b. The unborn can be used as a dependent child if ( 402-1 ):

i. The boyfriend has acknowledged paternity by a signed Form 941; and

ii. The pregnancy is in the third trimester.

3. When determining eligibility for a child of a minor parent, the following apply:

a. Count the income and assets of the child's parents living in the home ( 229-1 ).

b. Do not count the income and assets of the child's grandparents living in the home.

4. When determining eligibility for married minor parents living with either of their parents, and both minor parents are requesting coverage, count the applicants' and the parents' income and assets to determine the minor parents' eligibility.

· Do not count the income of the parents with whom they are living to determine eligibility if only the minor parent is requesting coverage and that individual is not the child of the parents.

Example : Susan and Bob are married. Although they are both 16-years-old, they are emancipated through marriage. Susan and Bob live with Bob’s parents. Susan is pregnant and has filed an application for medical assistance. Bob does not want medical coverage for himself. First determine Susan's eligibility for a MAGI-based coverage group. If she does not qualify for a MAGI-based coverage group, determine her eligibility for medically needy pregnant woman based on her and Bob's income and assets. Do not count the income and assets of Bob's parents because Bob is not requesting medical coverage with Susan.

body:
Previous Policy (405-3 was previously found in 465-2 until November 1, 2021)

When a minor parent between age 18 and 19 does not qualify under a MAGI-based coverage group, determine eligibility for medically needy and whose income and assets to count based on the minor parent's school attendance, living situation and deprivation. If the child could qualify for CHIP and a medically needy coverage group, the child has the choice of programs.

A. Medically Needy Family or Child

1. Determine eligibility for a minor parent who meets the age criteria as defined in 345-1 as follows:

a. Determine eligibility for Medically Needy Family when the minor parent is deprived of support ( 345-2 ).

b. Determine eligibility for Medically Needy Child when the minor parent is not deprived of support.

c. Include the following individuals in the household size of the minor parent ( 405-2 ):

· the minor parent

· a spouse

· parents

· siblings

· children of the minor parent

· unborn children of anyone in the household size

d. Count the income and assets of the minor parent and spouse (if living in the home). Count the income of the parents. Do not deem income from their siblings or child.

2. When determining eligibility for Medically Needy Family for a minor parent who does not meet the age criteria in 345-1 , include only the minor parent, spouse and any children in the household. Only count the income and assets of the minor parent and spouse.

· Determine eligibility for the minor parent's child for MAGI-based Child Medicaid ( 347 ). If the child fails MAGI-based coverage, the child may be covered under the Medically Needy Family program ( 405-1 ).

3. The minor parent may be eligible for Medically Needy or CHIP. Allow the member to choose.

4. If the spouse lives with the minor parent, determine the spouse's eligibility first using the MAGI-based methodology ( 401-2 ). If the spouse is not eligible, determine eligibility under Medically Needy Family ( 405-1 ).

Example : Sara and Jim are both 18 and married. They are parents of Cody. They live with Sara's mother. Sara is deprived of support and meets the student criteria. She is not eligible under a MAGI-based group and wants medically needy Medicaid. Count her mother, herself, her spouse and their child in the household size. Deem income and assets from Sara's mother and Sara's spouse. If Jim wants Medicaid, determine his eligibility first under a MAGI-based coverage group. If he fails, he can be considered for family or child medically needy considering only his and Sara's income and assets.

B. Medically Needy Pregnant Woman Medicaid for the 18-year-old

If the 18-year-old is pregnant and fails the MAGI-based coverage groups, determine eligibility for medically needy Pregnant Woman Medicaid. Student status does not matter ( 349 ).

· Count her income and assets, and her spouse's, if he is living with her.

· Do not deem income and assets from her parents.

· Do not deem income and assets from the father of the baby if he is not married to the mother, even if he has established paternity.

· Count in the household, the number of unborn children of her or her spouse.

· See 503-2 for the asset limit.

body:
Previous Policy (408-1 was previously found in 475-1 until November 1, 2021)

A. The Aged and Disabled 100% Poverty-Related Medicaid

The following policies determine whether to use the 100% poverty rate for one or two persons.

B. Who to Include in the Household Size

The household size for medically needy Medicaid must include the following individuals:

1. Aged or disabled person.

2. Spouse. Note: A spouse is living in the same home if either the individual or the spouse is temporarily absent for schooling, vacation, work, or medical care as defined in 408-2 .

a. Aged, blind or disabled spouse.

i. Combine the income of both spouses when both spouses are included in the Medicaid coverage to compare to 100% of the federal poverty level (FPL) for a two-person household.

ii. Deem the income of the spouse if an aged, blind or disabled spouse is not included in the Medicaid coverage, as per deeming policy in Sec. 410-2 .

· Use a household size of two even if the spouse has no deemable income.

b. Spouse receives SSI.

· Include an SSI recipient spouse in the household size.

· Count any income other than the SSI payment of the SSI recipient spouse.

· Compare countable income to 100% of poverty for a household size of two.

c. Spouse who is not aged, blind or disabled.

· Deem the income of a spouse living in the same home who is not aged, blind or disabled if that spouse's deemable income is more than the spousal allocation on Table II .

d. Non-qualified non-citizen spouse

· If the spouse is not a qualified non-citizen, deem the income and assets of the non-qualified non-citizen spouse using regular deeming rules.

i. If the non-qualified spouse is aged, blind or disabled, the non-qualified non-citizen will be included in the household size, but cannot be on the Medicaid program (A non-qualified non-citizen can only receive emergency Medicaid services, if he or she meets all other eligibility criteria.) .

ii. If there the non-qualified non-citizen spouse has deemable income, include the non-qualified non-citizen spouse in the household size, but do not include the spouse in the medical coverage.

C. Who Not to Include in the Household Size

1. Do not include the sponsor of a non-citizen in the household size.

2. Do not include the spouse who is a resident of a medical institution, or is eligible under a HCB waiver.

3. Do not include the spouse who is living in the same home who is not aged, blind, or disabled if that spouse's deemable income is less than, or equal to, the Spousal Allocation on Table II .

body:
Previous Policy

A. Temporary Absence for ABD Medicaid and MCS Programs

1. General Rule

A person is temporarily absent when the person leaves the primary residence but intends to, and does return in the same month or the following month. Usually the person must have lived in the home at least one month before the absence begins. However, sometimes a permanent residence is the place where one or more household members live and to which the individual intends to return.

2. Intent

a. If the individual or family member returns by the end of the month after the absence began, do not develop intent. The absence was temporary because the person returned within the time limit.

b. If you learn someone has left the home before the end of the second month, ask the individual if the person intends to return by the end of the month after the absence began. Accept the client's statement.

c. If the individual says the absence is temporary, the person is still a resident of the household until the end of the month after the month the absence began. If the person has not returned by then, the absence is not temporary and the person is no longer part of the household. (See 3, 4 and 5 below for exceptions.)

d. If the individual says the absence is not temporary, stop counting the person in the household effective the month after the absence began. (See 3. below if the absent family member is a child away at school.)

e. If the individual enters a medical facility, see 6 below.

3. Child away at school

a. A child away at school (educational or vocational training facility) is temporarily absent from the parent's home if he returns some weekends, holidays, or vacations, and he is subject to parental control. In this case, the child is temporarily absent regardless of the duration of the absence. The child is still part of the parent's household. To determine how this impacts income deeming, see 410-5.

b. A child away at school who is not subject to parental control is not a resident of the parent's household. If the child is the eligible individual, determine where the child lives based on the type and location of his or her actual physical residence. If the child is an ineligible child, remove the child from the household. (See 410-5 )

c. The temporary absence ends when the child returns home.

d. The temporarily absent child stops being a part of the household when the child no longer intends to return home, or no longer meets the definition of a child. (See 410-5 if a non-disabled student is no longer a student.)

4. Child in private non-medical facility

A child living at a private non-medical facility that is not for education or vocational training is not temporarily absent if the child will not return by the end of the month after the absence begins. The child is a resident of the facility. The child becomes a resident of the facility at the beginning of the month after entering the facility when the stay will not end by the end of the second month. (See 410-5 for deeming policy)

5. Absence for military service

An ineligible spouse or parent who is absent due solely to active duty in the Armed Forces is temporarily absent if he or she intends to return to the home. The ineligible spouse or parent is still a resident of the household. Accept the client's statement or a statement from the ineligible spouse or parent.

6. Absence for medical treatment

The individual is temporarily absent if the individual returns before the end of the month in which the absence began.

· See 215-4 for additional information on when individuals enter a medical institution.

· See 410 for deeming policy.

· See 415-10 to decide what amount of in-kind shelter to count, if applicable.

7. Homeless

If a individual is homeless, see 215-2

body:
Previous Policy (408-3 was previously found in 475-2 until November 1, 2021)

A. The Medically Needy Household

Individuals eligible for the Medically Needy (spenddown) program for aged, blind and disabled persons will spenddown to 100% of the federal poverty guideline for the applicable household size. The following policies determine whether to use the poverty rate for one or two persons.

B. Who to include in the household size

The household size for medically needy Medicaid must include the following individuals:

1. The aged, blind or disabled person.

2. Spouse living in the same home.

Note: A spouse is living in the same home if either the individual or the spouse is temporarily absent for schooling, vacation, work, or medical care as defined in 408-2

a. Aged, blind or disabled spouse.

i. Combine the income of both spouses to compare to 100% of poverty for a two-person household size to determine the spenddown amount when both spouses want Medicaid coverage.

ii. Deem income of the spouse per policy in Sec. 410-6 when only one spouse wants coverage and has deemable income.

· Count the spouse in the household size and use the income limit for two if the spouse has deemable income.

· Do not count the spouse in the household size and use the income limit for one if the spouse does not have deemable income.

b. Spouse receives SSI.

i. Include an SSI recipient spouse in the household size.

ii. Do not count the SSI spouse's income

iii. Compare countable income to 100% of poverty for one person to determine eligibility for the non-SSI spouse.

c. Spouse who is not aged, blind or disabled.

· Deem income of a spouse who is not aged, blind or disabled if that spouse's deemable income is more than the Spousal Allocation on Table II . (See Sec. 410-2 .) The spouse is included in the household size only if the spouse has deemable income.

d. Non-qualified non-citizen spouse.

· Deem the income of a non-qualified non-citizen spouse with deemable income following deeming rules in Sec. 410-2 . Also count assets of the non-qualified non-citizen spouse.

· If there is deemable income, include the non-qualified non-citizen in the household size (BMS), but not in the Medicaid coverage.

C. Who Not to Include in the Household Size

1. Do not include the sponsor of a non-citizen in the household size.

2. Do not include a spouse who is a resident of a medical institution or is eligible under a HCB waiver.

3. Do not include a spouse who is aged, blind or disabled and does not want coverage if that spouse's deemable income is less than, or equal to, the Spousal Allocation on Table II . (See Sec. 410-2 )

4. Do not include a spouse who is living in the same home who is not aged, blind, or disabled if that spouse's deemable income is less than, or equal to, the Spousal Allocation on Table II . (See Sec. 410-2 )

5. Do not include parents or siblings of a disabled child.

body:
Previous Policy

A. Who to Include in the Household Size

The household size for a QMB, SLMB, or QI case must include the following individuals:

1. Medicare recipient.

2. Spouse living in the same home. Note: A spouse is living in the same home if either the individual or the spouse is temporarily absent for schooling, vacation, work, or medical care.

a. A spouse who receives Part A Medicare:

i. A spouse who receives Part A Medicare may be included in the coverage or not included in the coverage, depending on the individual's choice.

ii. If the spouse wants coverage, combine the income of both and compare it to the applicable percentage of poverty for two.

iii. If the spouse does not want coverage, their income will be deemed according to the rules in 410-2 .

iv. In both situations, use the two-person household size and income limit. Also follow these procedures when one spouse is eligible under a waiver, and both are Medicare Part A eligible.

b. An aged, blind or disabled spouse who does not have Part A Medicare.

i. The income of a spouse who does not have Part A Medicare must be deemed including a spouse eligible under a waiver.

ii. Use a household size of two.

iii. Deem income from the spouse according to the rules in 410-2 .

c. If the spouse is not a qualified non-citizen, but is aged, blind or disabled, deem the income and assets of the non-qualified non-citizen spouse using regular deeming rules.

· The non-qualified non-citizen will be included in the household size, but cannot be included on the QMB/SLMB/QI program even if the non-citizen spouse receives Medicare.

d. A spouse who is not aged, blind or disabled if that spouse's deemable income is more than the Spousal Allocation on Table II : (See 410-2 )

i. If the spouse does not meet citizenship/non-citizen status requirements found in 205 , deem the income and assets of the non-citizen spouse using regular deeming rules.

ii. If there is deemable income, the non-citizen spouse will be counted in the household size, but cannot be included in the QM coverage.

e. Do not include a spouse who is a resident of a medical institution.

f. If one spouse is receiving Medicaid under a Home and Community Based Waiver and the other does not, first determine eligibility for QMB/SLMB together when both have Medicare Part A and both want coverage.

g. A Medicaid eligible spouse with deemable income must be deemed to the QI program for their spouse, but cannot be included in the QI coverage.

B. Who not to Include in the Household Size

1. Do not include the sponsor of a non-citizen in the household size.

2. Do not include a spouse who is a resident of a medical institution.

3. Do not include a spouse who is living in the same home who does not receive Part A Medicare and is not aged, blind or disabled if that spouse's deemable income is less than, or equal to, the Spousal Allocation on Table II . (See 410-2 )

4. Do not include parents or siblings in the household size of a Medicare recipient child.

body:
Previous Policy (408-5 was previously found in 475-4 until November 1, 2021)

A. The Medicaid Work Incentive Program

The following policies determine who to include in the household size when comparing income to the 250% poverty rate.

B. Who Must be Included in the Household Size?

The household size for medically needy Medicaid must include the following individuals:

1. The disabled person

2. A spouse living in the home:

a. If the spouse is disabled and also qualifies for the program include the spouse in the MWI coverage.

b. If the spouse does not qualify for the Work Incentive program, their income must be deemed.

c. If the spouse receives SSI, their income does not count.

3. The parent of a minor individual living in the home:

a. Parents’ income is deemed.

b. If one parent receives SSI, both parents’ income is excluded.

4. Minor children of a disabled individual and siblings of a disabled minor individual.

· Also include children and siblings up to age 21 who are full-time students. (When a child turns 18, and is no longer a full-time student, change the child's status in the household so they are no longer included.)

C. Who Not to Include in the Household Size

1. Do not include the sponsor of a non-citizen.

2. Do not include a spouse, child or sibling who is a resident of a medical institution, or who is eligible under a HCB waiver.

body:
B. Temporary Absence for ABD Medicaid

1. General Rule

A person is temporarily absent when the person leaves the primary residence but intends to, and does return in the same month or the following month. Usually the person must have lived in the home at least one month before the absence begins. However, sometimes a permanent residence is the place where one or more household members live and to which the individual intends to return.

If a individual is homeless, see 215-2 .

2. Intent

a. If the individual or family member returns by the end of the month after the absence began, do not develop intent. The absence was temporary because the person returned within the time limit.

b. If you learn someone has left the home before the end of the second month, ask the individual if the person intends to return by the end of the month after the absence began. Accept the client's statement.

c. If the individual says the absence is temporary, the person is still a resident of the household until the end of the month after the month the absence began. If the person has not returned by then, the absence is not temporary and the person is no longer part of the household. (See 3, 4 and 5 below for exceptions.)

d. If the individual says the absence is not temporary, stop counting the person in the household effective the month after the absence began. (See 3. below if the absent family member is a child away at school.)

e. If the individual enters a medical facility, see 6 below.

3. Child away at school

a. A child away at school (educational or vocational training facility) is temporarily absent from the parent's home if they return some weekends, holidays, or vacations, and they are subject to parental control. In this case, the child is temporarily absent regardless of the duration of the absence. The child is still part of the parent's household. To determine how this impacts income deeming, see 410-3 .

b. A child away at school who is not subject to parental control is not a resident of the parent's household. If the child is the eligible individual, determine where the child lives based on the type and location of his or her actual physical residence. If the child is an ineligible child, remove the child from the household. (See 410-3 )

c. The temporary absence ends when the child returns home.

d. The temporarily absent child stops being a part of the household when the child no longer intends to return home, or no longer meets the definition of a child. (See 408-2 if a non-disabled student is no longer a student.)

4. Child in non-medical facility

A child living at a non-medical facility that is not the Utah State Hospital and is not for education or vocational training is not temporarily absent if the child will not return by the end of the month after the absence begins. The child is a resident of the facility. The child becomes a resident of the facility at the beginning of the month after entering the facility when the stay will not end by the end of the second month. (See 410-3 for deeming policy)

5. Absence for military service

An ineligible spouse or parent who is absent due solely to active duty in the Armed Forces is temporarily absent if they intend to return to the home. The ineligible spouse or parent is still a resident of the household. Accept the client's statement or a statement from the ineligible spouse or parent.

6. Absence for medical treatment

The individual is temporarily absent if the individual returns before the end of the month in which the absence began. See 410-3 for deeming policy. See 415-10 to decide what amount of in-kind shelter to count, if applicable. See 215-2 for additional information on when individuals enter a medical institution.
citation_label: Utah DHHS Medicaid Policy Manual: 408-6 ABD - Joint Custody and Temporary Absence 3
heading: 4. If there is an actual change of residence of a Medicaid recipient (child begins living in the other parent's household more than 50% of the time), remove the child from the open Medicaid case using 10-10-10 rules. If the other parent has an open medical assistance case, refer to 815-4 about adding a new household member to re-determine the child's eligibility.

body:
Previous Policy ( 409 was previously found in 485 until November 1, 2021)

General Income Counting Concepts

Count income of the eligible individual to determine eligibility for Medicaid.

· If the individual has a spouse, the spouse's income is deemed available to the individual; however, the process of counting a spouse's income depends on a number of factors based on the program.

· If the eligible individual is a child under age 18, count the child's income as well as the income deemed from the parents.

· Refer to section 410-2 and 410-3 for policy on how to deem income from a spouse or a parent.

For Medicare Cost Sharing programs, count the Medicare recipient's income.

· If both spouses receive Medicare and both want coverage, include the spouse's income.

· Deem income from an ineligible spouse, or ineligible parent of an eligible, dependent child following policy in 410-2 and 410-3 .

The Medicaid Work Incentive program applies different rules on how to count income from a spouse or a parent. Refer to section 314 for this policy.

The sections listed below have detailed information about how to count income to determine an individual's eligibility.

· Medicaid for SSI Recipients and SSI Protected Groups ( 409-1 )

· Aged and Disabled Poverty-Related Medicaid, QMB, SLMB, and QI ( 409-2 )

· Aged, Blind and Disabled Medically Needy Medicaid ( 409-3 )

Previous Policy (409-1 was previously found in 485-1 until November 1, 2021)

A. Individuals who Receive SSI or a State Supplemental Payment (SSP)

Do not count any income for individuals who receive SSI or a State Supplemental Payment (SSP).

B. Individuals on Disabled Adult Child Medicaid

Do not count any income to decide an individual’s eligibility if:

· They meet the criteria of the Disabled Adult Child protected group, and

· They pass the income test described in 330-1 ,

C. Individuals on Pickle Amendment and Disabled Widows/Widowers Medicaid

Disabled Widows and people eligible because of the Pickle Amendment require the following income calculation.

1. Deem income from the individual’s spouse or parent.

2. If the person passes the income calculation for the protected group they qualify for Medicaid without a spenddown.

D. Individuals on 1619(a) or 1619(b) Medicaid

Do not count any income for individuals who are in 1619(a) or 1619(b) status. They are "income eligible" for Medicaid.
